mechanism_sources.title: NHGRI: Gene–environment interaction
mechanism_sources.scope: Conceptual distinction between genetic liability and environmental influences; not evidence for a nutrition-to-genetic-risk edge.

chapters.reason: Inherited genetic variants can influence brain development and systems involved in attention and impulse regulation. Greater genetic susceptibility can therefore increase the likelihood of ADHD, without determining whether a particular person develops it.
examples: Mira is born with higher inherited susceptibility to ADHD. As everyday demands increase, persistent attention and impulse-control difficulties become noticeable; the inherited susceptibility is a possible contributor, not a certain outcome.

Noah and a sibling grow up in the same household but inherit different combinations of genetic variants. In this fictional example, greater ADHD susceptibility helps explain why one develops persistent difficulties while the other does not.

chapters.reason: Here ADHD must mean the underlying condition, not the act of receiving a diagnosis. Difficulties regulating attention and impulses are expressed as symptoms; a greater underlying burden can mean more frequent or disruptive symptoms, although this is partly a description of the condition rather than an independent causal mechanism.
examples: Mira wants to follow a classroom assignment, but attention repeatedly shifts before the instructions are complete. This example makes the underlying attention-regulation difficulty visible as persistent symptoms, rather than suggesting that a diagnostic label created them.

During a group activity, Noah repeatedly speaks before others finish despite trying to wait. The difficulty regulating impulses appears as a more frequent symptom, not a deliberate decision to be disruptive.

chapters.reason: More frequent attention or impulse-control difficulties can interrupt following instructions, organizing work and completing activities. The symptom becomes functional impairment when it prevents someone from doing something they need or want to do.
examples: Mira understands the classroom assignment, but repeatedly loses a place in the instructions and starts again. By the deadline the work is unfinished, so an attention difficulty has become a practical obstacle.

Noah keeps interrupting during a group activity and misses the agreed next step. The group cannot finish the shared task smoothly, showing how a symptom can affect participation rather than just appear on a checklist.

chapters.reason: When daily activities become harder to complete, they can take time and energy away from relationships, enjoyment and independence. Greater disruption can therefore reduce quality of life, although support and other circumstances can soften that effect.
examples: An unfinished classroom assignment follows Mira into the evening. While friends play outside, Mira stays behind to catch up; the cost is missing something personally meaningful, not just unfinished work.
Noah repeatedly struggles to organize the day and cancels a long-awaited outing to deal with overdue responsibilities. The practical difficulty narrows opportunities for enjoyment and connection.
